blocks.text: This aesthetic arose as a direct response to both the widespread minimalist trend of the 2010s as well as the COVID-19 lockdown of 2020. The 2010s saw the rise of Minimalism, Scandinavian design, and Japandi, and with that, a cultural design shift towards simple, sophisticated interiors, industrial accents, and neutral-to-beige color palettes. Generation Z systemically rejected this, finding it restrictive, and embraced all things maximalist instead, in both fashion and interior design. This can be seen in the bold color combinations, eye-catching patterns, and asymmetrical, often cluttered, decorations.

Danish Pastel was also a result of the global lockdowns of 2020 caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Many sought to redesign their interior spaces due to being constantly confined to them, and desired a more optimistic, comforting design style to counter the chaos of the world outside. For some, bringing colors like bright blue and soft yellow into the home was an attempt to re-experience the beauty of nature that was being withheld from them due to the lockdown.
Much of this aesthetic takes inspiration from modern art that emphasizes shapes in flat colors, such as works by Matisse and Picasso.

Danish Pastel prioritizes pairing fun, childlike, and abstract elements with Scandi and Scandi-inspired furniture. It overtly emphasizes a bright pastel color palette, but also highlights whimsy by mixing patterns and including organic shapes wherever possible. Decorative elements such as pillows, vases, candles, and mirror frames are often characterized by playful, fluid forms. These organic forms contrast with the rigidity of the patterns often found in this style. Likewise, checkerboard, stripes, and grid patterns dominate this aesthetic, adding structure to the otherwise soft sensibilities of the trend.

Of course, pastels are the focal point of the aesthetic. These are typically bright or "neon" pastels rather than pale ones, with the most common colors being pink, lilac, baby blue, soft yellow, green, and white. Though it can go in a more minimalist direction, the trend encourages lots of layered decor in the home, often mixing colors and prints recklessly. Gallery walls, bookshelves lined with books and trinkets, and floating scalloped shelves topped with vases and plants are common sights in the Danish Pastel home. Here is a list of popular furniture and decor pieces utilized in Danish Pastel:
Twist, swirly, bubble cube, rainbow-shaped and S- or U-shaped candles
Tiled, cubed planters, boxes, and vases
Pastel posters, with simplistic and cutesy but colorful designs of flowers, fruits, abstractions, etc.
Hearts (most notably Powerpuff Girls-inspired heart patterns)

Around the same time that the interior design style became popular, fashion trends with the same elements also developed. Pastels were seeing a popularity boom in general, with Soft Boy and Soft Girl emerging in 2019, making it easy for people to translate the interior design aesthetic into fashion. The style is closest to Avant Basic visually, and there tends to be some crossover between the two both stylistically and design-wise. In terms of garments and silhouettes, the aesthetic follows contemporary trends of 2023. It also introduces color blocking, argyle, and gingham as additional patterns for clothing.

Critics of Danish Pastel dislike the trends' "cute-ification" of its sophisticated predecessor, Scandinavian design, and say it removes the intentional complexity and depth of the style in favor of trendy childlike colors and imagery. Some say there is more Japanese influence in this aesthetic than Scandinavian, and very little Danish design included at all, expressing confusion over the name of the aesthetic.
